notes.meaning: People from all over the land, from Dan in the far north to Beersheba in the south and Gilead east of the Jordan, gathered as one united body at Mizpah. They assembled before the Lord to deal with the terrible crime committed at Gibeah. Their shared outrage brought the nation together with a single purpose.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Cambridge Bible suggests that one strand of the text places the gathering at Mizpah while another places it at Bethel.

notes.meaning: The leaders of all the tribes took their places to guide the assembly of God's people. An army of 400,000 armed foot soldiers stood ready to act. The leaders are called cornerstones because they hold the nation together the way foundation stones support a building.

The tribe of Benjamin heard that the rest of Israel had gathered at Mizpah, but they chose to stay away. The assembled tribes then opened the council by asking for a full report of how this wicked deed happened. They wanted to examine the facts directly before taking any action.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Cambridge Bible suggests that the first half of this verse interrupts the flow of the story and originally belonged before verse 14.

notes.meaning: The Levite stood before the assembly to give his account of the murder of his concubine. He explained that he had only stopped in Gibeah, a town in Benjamin, to spend the night as a peaceful traveler. He made it clear which town was responsible so that innocent cities would not be blamed.

The Levite stated that the men of Gibeah surrounded the house at night and intended to kill him. He explained that they abused his concubine until she died from the attack. While his report described their terrible violence, he highlighted his own danger and passed over how he had pushed the woman out to the mob.

The Levite explained why he cut the woman's body into pieces and sent them across the land. He wanted every tribe to witness the depth of the wickedness done in Israel. Such shocking sexual violence was a direct violation of God's covenant law and could not be ignored.

The Levite called on all the people of Israel to give their counsel and reach a verdict right there. Because they were God's covenant people, the duty fell on them to uphold justice and clear the land of evil.
The entire assembly rose up with one voice and vowed not to return home until this wickedness was punished. They put the pursuit of justice and God's honor ahead of their private lives and comfort.
The Israelites resolved to march against Gibeah and cast lots to direct their attack. This approach treated the wicked city like a corrupt Canaanite town marked for total destruction under God's law.

The assembly chose one man out of every ten to gather food and supplies for the army. This practical step ensured the 400,000 soldiers would not scatter to look for food during a long campaign. Proper planning helps people follow through on their commitments to do what is right.
All the men of Israel gathered together against Gibeah, completely united in purpose. They showed that true unity is meant to be used for defending justice and opposing evil.

Before attacking, the tribes sent messengers throughout the territory of Benjamin to confront them about the crime. They wanted to give their brothers a chance to hand over the guilty and avoid a full-scale war.

The messengers demanded that Gibeah hand over the wicked men so they could be put to death and the evil removed from Israel. Instead of obeying God's law, the tribe of Benjamin refused to listen to their brothers. By shielding the criminals from justice, Benjamin made itself guilty of the very same sin.

The soldiers of Benjamin left their hometowns and gathered at Gibeah to fight against the rest of Israel. What should have been the punishment of a few guilty men turned into a tragic civil war between brothers.
Benjamin mustered 26,000 swordsmen from their cities, in addition to 700 chosen men from Gibeah. Even though their army was tiny compared to the rest of Israel, stubborn pride drove them to fight.

Among Benjamin's forces were 700 elite left-handed slingers who could sling a stone at a hair without missing. In ancient battle, left-handed slingers had a major tactical advantage because their stones struck an enemy's unshielded right side.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Douay-Rheims translation describes these warriors as fighting with the left hand as well as with the right, understanding them to be ambidextrous.

notes.meaning: The other tribes of Israel gathered an army of 400,000 experienced swordsmen. This gave Israel an overwhelming numerical advantage of roughly fifteen to one over Benjamin.

The Israelites went to Bethel to ask God which tribe should lead the attack, and the Lord chose Judah. Israel felt so confident in their numbers and their righteous cause that they asked only about battle order rather than asking if they should go to war at all.
The Israelite army got up early the next morning and set up their military camp near Gibeah. They marched directly toward the city where the terrible crime had taken place.
The men of Israel marched out and drew up their battle lines against Benjamin outside Gibeah. They took up their combat positions to face their own countrymen in open war.

The Benjaminites charged out of Gibeah and struck down 22,000 Israelite soldiers on that single day. God allowed this crushing defeat because Israel was relying on human strength and fighting in self-righteous pride without dealing with their own sins.

Despite the terrible loss of life, the Israelite soldiers encouraged one another and drew up their battle lines in the exact same place as the first day. They refused to give up, relying on their remaining numbers and their determination to avenge their defeat.

Before attacking again, the Israelites went up to Bethel and wept before the Lord until evening. They asked whether they should fight their brother Benjamin, and God told them to go up, though He still did not promise them victory. Israel needed to be thoroughly humbled before God would give them success.
On the second day of fighting, the army of Israel advanced once more against Benjamin. Even when people set out to correct evil, doing the right thing can involve deep pain and hardship.
